headerBody: Sourced from Japanese police and consumer-agency records — the Tokyo Metropolitan Police, the National Consumer Affairs Center (hotline 188), and the Nara Prefectural Government — plus r/JapanTravel reports and verified local news. The exact scripts, the red flags, and the Japanese phrases that shut each scam down on the spot.
quadHead: Four ways Japan catches tourists off guard.

quad.title: The Kabukicho Bottakuri Bar
quad.tl: A tout waves you into a “cheap drinks” bar; when the ¥80,000+ bill lands, four bouncers block the door. Shinjuku Police logged 190 cases in 2024.

quad.title: The Fake Monk’s Bracelet
quad.tl: A robed “monk” near Sensoji slips a gold bracelet onto your wrist as a “gift,” then opens a donation book for ¥3,000–¥10,000. Real monks don’t solicit on the street.

quad.title: The Otoshi Cover Charge
quad.tl: The little dish you never ordered? In Gion’s worst izakayas, “otoshi” plus hidden seat charges quietly stack ¥3,000+ onto the bill.

quad.title: The Nara Park Deer
quad.tl: The “bowing” deer turn the instant the ¥200 crackers appear — head-butts, bites, gored thighs. The prefecture logged 159 injuries in 2024.

body: Japan: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against Japanese police and consumer-agency records — the Tokyo Metropolitan Police, the National Consumer Affairs Center (188), and the Nara Prefectural Government — plus r/JapanTravel reports and verified local news. Not a recycled blog list.

60 specific scams across Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, Sapporo and five more cities. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the Japanese phrases that shut them down — with kana and romaji you can show on your phone.

Scams evolve, so the book is re-researched and updated every year — when a new edition ships, it appears in your Kindle library. Built for the traveler who wants to move through Japan relaxed, not braced.
